summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for parallel-printer-like hardware devices. It was replaced by RFC 1660.

eli5.summary: A list of things you can check about a printer connection, like whether it is ready, using the same standard questions for any printer maker.

questions: how to monitor printer ports with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management objects for parallel printer ports

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to monitor and manage parallel printer ports on networked devices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of SNMP managed objects that report the status of parallel-printer-like hardware ports, including information about input and output control signals like power, online status, busy state, paper out, and fault conditions.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can use SNMP to remotely check printer port status, detect problems, and monitor changes. This RFC was replaced by RFC 1660, which provides an updated specification.

today: RFC 1318 defined the Parallel-printer-like MIB but is now obsolete. It was replaced by RFC 1660, which provides an updated specification for parallel printer device management.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1318 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management of parallel-printer-like devices. It provides a standard set of managed objects that network management protocols, such as SNMP, can use to monitor and configure parallel printer ports.

The most common examples are Centronics and Data Products type parallel printer ports found on routers, print servers, and other network devices. These ports connect directly to physical printers or peripherals and often include status signals that indicate the printer's condition.
sections.eli5: This document creates a standard way to ask questions about a printer's parallel port connection, the same way you might check on a printer in person.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework consists of three main components. RFC 1155 defines the Structure of Management Information (SMI), which is the formal language used to describe managed objects. RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects that all Internet devices should support.

The framework also includes RFC 1157, which defines SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). SNMP is the protocol that management stations use to query and modify managed objects on remote devices. The Parallel-printer-like MIB builds on this framework, adding objects specific to parallel printer ports.
sections.eli5: SNMP is like a standardized form that network administrators fill out to ask a device questions. This document adds a new section to the form, specifically for asking about printer ports.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Objects
sections.content:
The Parallel-printer-like MIB is one of a set of complementary MIBs designed for different hardware types. It complements the Character MIB (for terminal-like interfaces), the PPP MIB (for point-to-point links), and the RS-232-like MIB (for serial ports). Together, they form a layered approach where physical-level MIBs represent the lowest level, and higher-level MIBs represent applications using those ports.

The MIB comprises one base object (paraNumber) and three tables: a port table (paraPortTable) with port index and type information, an input signal table (paraInSigTable) tracking incoming status signals, and an output signal table (paraOutSigTable) tracking outgoing control signals. These objects apply to both Centronics and Data Products parallel connections with similar control signal sets.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a filing cabinet. The base object counts how many parallel ports exist. The three tables are like drawers that hold details about each port and its signals.

sections.title: Port Signals and Status
sections.content:
The MIB tracks five key hardware signals that indicate printer status. Input signals (from the printer to the device) include Power (device has electrical power), Online (printer is online and ready), Busy (printer is processing a job), PaperOut (paper tray is empty), and Fault (hardware malfunction). Output signals (from the device to the printer) include the same five types, representing control commands the device can send.

For each signal, the MIB records the current state (on, off, or not available) and a counter tracking how many times the signal has changed from on to off or vice versa. This allows administrators to see not just the current status, but also detect patterns of problems. For example, a Fault signal that toggles frequently suggests an intermittent hardware issue.
sections.eli5: The MIB watches five lights: is it plugged in, ready, busy, out of paper, or broken. For each one, it records whether the light is on or off, and counts how many times it blinks.

sections.title: Use and Applicability
sections.content:
The Parallel-printer-like MIB is mandatory for all systems that have parallel printer ports supporting services managed through other MIBs, such as the Character MIB. Because parallel ports vary in their capabilities, the MIB includes objects not applicable to all port types. Objects specific to certain hardware types are in a separate branch of the MIB tree and are required only when applicable.

Network administrators use the MIB to build monitoring and alerting systems. A management station can poll port status periodically, detect when a printer goes offline or out of paper, and generate alerts. The signal change counters help identify flaky hardware that frequently alternates between working and not working states.
sections.eli5: Not every device has every type of parallel port, so the MIB is designed to support only the signals that a particular port actually has. Administrators use this information to fix printer problems before users even notice them.
